title: ISACA Certified in Risk and Information Systems Control (CRISC)
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the ISACA CRISC exam content outline (four official domains and weightings). Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: An organization is defining how it will oversee technology-related decisions and risks. Which body should ultimately be accountable for setting the enterprise risk appetite and ensuring it is reflected in IT strategy?
options: The board of directors through its governance structure
The IT operations manager responsible for daily uptime
The external service provider that hosts the systems
The internal audit team during its annual review
items.explanation: Setting risk appetite and aligning it with strategy is a governance responsibility owned by the board, which is accountable to stakeholders. Operations, vendors, and internal audit support or provide assurance but do not own appetite.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Management is documenting the amount of risk the organization is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives. What term describes this formally stated level of acceptable risk?
options: Residual risk
Risk appetite
Risk tolerance
Risk capacity
items.explanation: Risk appetite is the broad amount and type of risk the organization is willing to accept to achieve its objectives. Tolerance is the acceptable variation around that appetite, capacity is the maximum it could absorb, and residual risk is what remains after controls.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: A business unit routinely exceeds the variance limits that senior management set around its target risk position. Which concept have those limits exceeded?
options: Risk capacity
Inherent risk
Risk tolerance
Risk appetite
items.explanation: Tolerance is the acceptable deviation from the risk appetite or target. Exceeding the tolerance signals the position has moved outside the agreed band and should trigger escalation, rather than being confused with the overall appetite or capacity.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Before approving a major expansion, the board must understand the maximum amount of risk the organization could absorb before suffering unacceptable loss. Which concept does this describe?
options: Risk appetite
Risk tolerance
Control risk
Risk capacity
items.explanation: Risk capacity is the maximum risk an organization can take on before insolvency or unacceptable harm to its objectives. It is an outer limit that sits above the appetite the board actually chooses to operate within.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between enterprise governance and IT governance?
options: IT governance is a subset of enterprise governance that directs and controls IT to support enterprise objectives
IT governance is fully independent of enterprise governance and sets its own strategy
IT governance supersedes enterprise governance for all technology decisions
Enterprise governance reports to the IT steering committee for approval
items.explanation: IT governance is the part of overall corporate governance that directs and controls technology so it supports enterprise goals. It cannot be independent of, or superior to, the governance of the whole organization.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: An organization wants independent assurance that risk management and internal controls are effective. Under a three lines of defense model, which function provides this assurance?
options: The board of directors directly
Internal audit as the third line
Business management as the first line
The risk and compliance function as the second line
items.explanation: In the three lines of defense model, operations own and manage risk, risk and compliance oversee it, and internal audit provides independent assurance to the governing body. The board receives the assurance rather than producing it.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: A document states that financial data must use AES-256 encryption at rest, and a separate document lists the step-by-step actions for applying it. How should these two documents be classified?
options: The encryption mandate is a policy and the step-by-step document is a standard
Both documents are procedures because both can be executed
The encryption mandate is a standard and the step-by-step document is a procedure
Both documents are policies because both contain mandatory wording
items.explanation: A policy states high-level intent and management direction, a standard states a specific mandatory requirement such as AES-256, and a procedure gives the detailed steps to carry it out. The two documents therefore map to a standard and a procedure.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: A project sponsor is preparing a justification for a security investment that weighs costs, benefits, and risks. What is this document called?
options: A risk register
A control matrix
An audit charter
A business case
items.explanation: A business case quantifies the costs and expected benefits of an investment so decision makers can compare it against alternatives and risk appetite. A risk register, control matrix, and audit charter serve different governance purposes.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Before onboarding a critical cloud vendor, what should the risk practitioner ensure is performed FIRST?
options: A due diligence assessment of the vendor's controls, security posture, and financial stability
Immediate signing of a multi-year contract to secure pricing
Delegation of all risk decisions to the vendor
Removal of the vendor from the enterprise risk register
items.explanation: Third-party risk begins with due diligence so the organization understands the vendor's control environment and stability before relying on it. Signing first, delegating decisions, or removing oversight all increase exposure without informed acceptance.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: In the accounts payable process, the same employee can both create a new vendor record and approve payments to it. Which governance control is missing?
options: Least privilege
Segregation of duties
Mandatory vacation
Job rotation
items.explanation: Segregation of duties prevents one person from controlling all steps of a transaction that could conceal fraud, such as creating a vendor and paying it. Least privilege limits access scope, while vacation and rotation are fraud-detection supplements, not the direct remedy here.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Which practice best demonstrates that IT strategy is aligned with enterprise strategy?
options: IT always purchases the newest technology available
The CIO avoids business involvement in technology planning
IT objectives are derived from and reviewed against business objectives
IT independently sets its own goals without business input
items.explanation: Alignment exists when technology objectives descend from and are measured against enterprise goals in a recurring review. Buying new technology, planning in isolation, or excluding the business from planning does not create alignment.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Employees at all levels consistently escalate concerns even when they fear blame. Which aspect of governance does this reflect?
options: Risk transfer
Risk aggregation
Risk capacity
A healthy risk culture
items.explanation: A strong risk culture encourages open reporting and escalation without fear, so issues surface early. Risk transfer, aggregation, and capacity are technical risk concepts and do not describe willingness to report concerns.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: An organization follows a regulation because it is the law, but it also improves controls beyond the minimum to reduce risk. Which statement best distinguishes compliance from risk management?
options: Compliance is meeting requirements, while risk management optimizes risk to achieve objectives
Compliance and risk management are the same activity
Compliance fully replaces the need for risk management
Risk management exists only to satisfy regulators
items.explanation: Compliance is a floor set by external requirements, whereas risk management is a broader, objective-driven discipline that may go beyond the minimum where exposure warrants. Treating them as identical, or as substitutes, misses this distinction.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Who is best positioned to be accountable for the quality and protection of a specific data domain?
options: The network engineer who manages connectivity
A designated data owner within the business accountable for that domain
The database administrator who maintains the servers
The external auditor who reviews controls
items.explanation: Data governance assigns accountability to a business-side data owner who understands the data's value and use. Administrators, auditors, and engineers support that ownership but are not accountable for the domain.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: A critical application cannot meet a new control standard before the deadline, so management documents the reason and gains approval to proceed anyway. What is this called?
options: A risk transfer
An audit finding
A policy exception
A control failure
items.explanation: A documented, authorized deviation from a standard is a policy exception, and it should have an owner, an expiry, and a compensating control. A control failure is an unintended breakdown, not an approved deviation.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Every key control recorded in the risk register should have which attribute to ensure clear accountability?
options: A purchase order number
A backup copy on tape
A marketing description
A named control owner
items.explanation: Each control needs a named owner responsible for its operation and testing. Purchase orders, backups, and marketing text do not establish accountability for whether the control works.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: What is the primary purpose of an enterprise risk committee?
options: To oversee risk across the enterprise and escalate material risks to the board
To perform daily transaction processing for the finance team
To sell insurance products to customers
To conduct external financial audits
items.explanation: An enterprise risk committee provides cross-functional oversight of risk and ensures material exposures reach the board. Processing transactions, selling insurance, and external auditing are separate functions.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: To preserve independence, to whom should the chief risk officer ideally have a direct reporting line?
options: The external audit firm
The board or a board-level risk committee
The head of IT operations
The sales director
items.explanation: Independence is preserved when the risk function reports directly to the board or a board committee. Reporting to an operational or commercial executive creates a conflict that can suppress the escalation of bad news.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Management is evaluating whether to enter a new business line that introduces residual risk above the stated appetite. What should the risk practitioner recommend?
options: Approve it, because residual risk is always lower than inherent risk
Ignore the appetite limit because the activity is profitable
Escalate the decision to the board and define treatment, or decline the activity
Proceed, because risk appetite is only informal guidance
items.explanation: When residual risk exceeds the appetite, the decision must move to the authority that can change the appetite or approve the exception. Proceeding on profit alone or treating appetite as optional defeats the governance purpose.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: A contract with a critical outsourcing provider should include which clause to protect the organization?
options: A clause forbidding any performance reporting
Automatic renewal without any review
Exclusion of all service level definitions
The right to audit the provider and to receive prompt breach notifications
items.explanation: Right-to-audit and breach-notification clauses preserve visibility and control over an outsourced service. Preventing reporting, auto-renewing without review, and removing service levels all reduce the organization's ability to manage the risk.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: An organization moves a core service to the public cloud. Which governance concern is most important to address FIRST?
options: Clarifying accountability for data and the division of controls under shared responsibility
Selecting the color scheme of the vendor's management console
Planning the annual marketing campaign
Confirming the location of the vendor's sales offices
items.explanation: Cloud adoption shifts who operates which controls, so governance must first establish accountability for data and the shared responsibility boundary. Cosmetic and commercial details do not address the core risk.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Which risk most directly increases when an organization outsources a critical function without appropriate oversight?
options: Guaranteed regulatory compliance
Loss of control over the service and the data it handles
Reduced need for any governance
Complete elimination of operational risk
items.explanation: Outsourcing transfers execution, not accountability, so weak oversight raises the risk of losing control over service quality and data. It cannot eliminate risk, remove governance, or guarantee compliance.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: An organization adopts COBIT to structure its technology governance. What does COBIT primarily provide?
options: A programming language for enterprise applications
A payroll and human resources system
A framework of governance and management objectives and processes
A mandatory hardware specification
items.explanation: COBIT is a governance framework that separates governance from management and supplies objectives and processes for directing and controlling enterprise IT. It is not a hardware spec, language, or business application.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: What should an organization establish FIRST when creating an enterprise risk management program?
options: A list of every conceivable threat that might occur
The purchase of insurance policies for all known exposures
The deployment of an intrusion detection system
A governance structure with clear ownership, appetite, and reporting lines
items.explanation: An ERM program needs governance first, so that risk ownership, appetite, and reporting are defined before tools or tactics are chosen. Threat lists, insurance, and detection tools support a program but do not establish it.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: The chief executive visibly prioritizes ethical behavior, accountability, and risk awareness. Which governance element does this represent?
options: Tone at the top
Control self-assessment
Risk transfer
Segregation of duties
items.explanation: Tone at the top refers to the culture and example set by senior leadership, which shapes how seriously the organization treats risk and ethics. Self-assessment, transfer, and segregation are specific mechanisms, not leadership culture.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: A regulator issues a new data protection rule. Which action best integrates it into governance?
options: Add it to the marketing plan as a promotional point
Translate the requirement into policies and assign accountable owners
Wait until a fine is issued before acting
Assign responsibility only to the IT help desk
items.explanation: Regulatory requirements become governable once translated into policies with assigned accountability and monitoring. Waiting, misassigning ownership, or repurposing it for marketing does not create compliance or control.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: What is the primary role of an IT steering committee?
options: To process the company payroll
To perform the annual financial audit
To prioritize and oversee IT investments and ensure they align with business strategy
To write and test application code
items.explanation: An IT steering committee is a governance forum that prioritizes technology investment and keeps it aligned with business direction. Coding, payroll, and auditing are operational or assurance activities outside its remit.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: How frequently should material risk information generally be presented to the board?
options: Only once at program inception
Never, to avoid concerning the board
Every day for every minor risk
At a defined cadence, with immediate escalation of significant changes
items.explanation: Board reporting follows an agreed cadence with immediate escalation for material changes, so oversight is timely without burying the board in trivia. One-time, never, or daily-for-everything are all ineffective.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: A limited budget forces a choice among competing risk treatments. What should guide the allocation?
options: Prioritization based on risk magnitude relative to appetite and expected benefit
The preference of the loudest manager in the room
Alphabetical order of the project names
The age of the legacy system regardless of exposure
items.explanation: Scarce resources should go where risk reduction is greatest relative to appetite and cost. Personal preference, alphabetical order, and system age are arbitrary and ignore exposure.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Who should have the authority to approve a policy exception that leaves high residual risk?
options: The external auditor reviewing the control
The governance body or executive accountable for the risk, within defined authority limits
Any developer on the team who is available
The newest employee needing to complete a task
items.explanation: Accepting high residual risk requires authority that matches the exposure, normally the accountable executive or governance body under an authority matrix. Delegating this to unavailable or unauthorized staff undermines accountability.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: What is the primary benefit of clearly assigning risk ownership?
options: It eliminates the risk entirely
It transfers all legal liability to the owner
It ensures a specific person is accountable for monitoring and treating the risk
It removes the need for any risk reporting
items.explanation: Naming an owner creates accountability for monitoring, treating, and reporting a risk. Ownership does not erase the risk, replace reporting, or shift legal liability.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Which action best keeps risk appetite aligned with corporate strategy?
options: Fixing the appetite permanently so it never changes
Allowing each unit to set an unlimited appetite
Setting the appetite to zero to avoid all risk
Setting risk limits that reflect strategic objectives and reviewing them as strategy changes
items.explanation: Appetite should be derived from strategy and revisited whenever strategy shifts. Freezing it, leaving it unlimited, or driving it to zero all disconnect appetite from the objectives it is meant to support.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: A multinational firm has inconsistent risk practices across its business units. Which governance approach best addresses this?
options: A common enterprise risk framework with consistent reporting and defined local responsibilities
Letting each unit invent a private method with no reporting
Banning all risk discussions outside headquarters
Outsourcing every unit's risk decisions to one vendor
items.explanation: A common framework with consistent reporting and local ownership gives comparable, reliable information across units. Fragmented methods, suppressed discussion, or blanket outsourcing all reduce the quality of governance.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Why would an organization use a capability maturity model for technology governance?
options: To calculate its tax liability
To assess current maturity and plan improvements in a structured way
To guarantee that no incident will ever occur
To replace all existing controls immediately
items.explanation: A maturity model provides a structured scale against which current capabilities are assessed and improvements planned. It cannot guarantee zero incidents, does not by itself replace controls, and has nothing to do with tax.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Which statement best distinguishes governance metrics from management metrics?
options: Governance metrics are always financial and management metrics never are
Management metrics are set by external auditors rather than leadership
Governance metrics show whether objectives and risk are overseen at the board level, while management metrics track operational performance
Governance metrics and management metrics are identical in scope
items.explanation: Governance metrics tell the board whether its direction is being achieved and risk overseen, while management metrics track the operational execution of that direction. They serve different audiences and purposes.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: What is the internal audit function's role in governance?
options: To manage day-to-day risk responses on behalf of management
To own and operate the organization's controls
To set the enterprise risk appetite for the board
To provide independent assurance on governance, risk management, and control
items.explanation: Internal audit supplies independent assurance to the board and does not manage or own controls, since doing so would compromise its independence. Setting appetite and executing responses are management and governance tasks.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: Which statement best describes integrating technology risk management with enterprise risk management?
options: Technology risk is assessed and reported within the enterprise risk framework rather than in isolation
Technology risk is deliberately kept entirely separate from enterprise risk
Enterprise risk management excludes all technology matters
Enterprise risk management applies only to financial reporting
items.explanation: Technology risk is a component of overall enterprise risk and should feed the same framework so it is aggregated and prioritized with all other risks. Silos hide the combined exposure from the board.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: During a merger, what is the MOST important risk governance activity before integration begins?
options: Deleting the target's historical records
Due diligence that assesses the target's risk profile and control environment
Immediately merging all IT systems without assessment
Announcing the deal terms to competitors
items.explanation: Due diligence reveals the target's inherent and control risk so the acquirer can plan integration and remediation. Rushing integration, leaking terms, or destroying records increases legal and operational risk.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: A business case is approved for a major initiative. What should governance ensure after approval?
options: That no changes to scope are permitted under any circumstances
That all progress reporting to management stops
That the projected benefits are tracked and the risks are monitored through delivery and operation
That the business case document is discarded immediately
items.explanation: Approval starts the accountability cycle, so benefits realization and risk monitoring continue through delivery and operation. Discarding the case, forbidding all change, and stopping reporting all defeat governance oversight.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Governance

items.stem: A risk practitioner is gathering information about events that could affect the achievement of objectives. What is this activity called?
options: Risk treatment
Risk transfer
Risk reporting
Risk identification
items.explanation: Risk identification is the step that surfaces the events and conditions that could affect objectives. Treatment, transfer, and reporting occur after risks are identified and analyzed.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: A system has a known weakness and no compensating controls in place. What term describes the risk level before any controls are applied?
options: Inherent risk
Residual risk
Control risk
Transferred risk
items.explanation: Inherent risk is the exposure that exists before controls are considered. Residual risk is what remains after controls, and control risk relates to controls failing to prevent or detect errors.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: After controls are implemented, management asks how much risk still remains. What is this remaining risk called?
options: Audit risk
Residual risk
Inherent risk
Detection risk
items.explanation: Residual risk is the exposure that remains after existing controls are taken into account. Inherent risk is the pre-control level, while detection and audit risk are assurance concepts.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Which set of attributes should a risk register record for each identified risk?
options: The color used in the printed report
The auditor's personal schedule
Description, likelihood, impact, owner, and planned response
Only the name of the risk and nothing else
items.explanation: A useful register captures the risk description along with likelihood, impact, ownership, and response so it can be prioritized, tracked, and reported. Storing only a name or irrelevant details provides no basis for decisions.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Which technique builds plausible sequences of events that could lead to an adverse business outcome?
options: Purchase requisition
Data archiving
Password reset
Scenario analysis
items.explanation: Scenario analysis constructs credible chains of events from cause to impact, helping teams reason about complex or emerging risks. The other options are administrative or technical actions unrelated to risk analysis.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: In a risk assessment, what does the combination of likelihood and impact typically represent?
options: The level or magnitude of the risk
The cost of the control
The audit fee for the engagement
The required recovery time
items.explanation: Likelihood and impact together express the magnitude or level of a risk and drive its prioritization. Control cost, audit fees, and recovery time are separate considerations, not the definition of risk level.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: A team compares identified risks against agreed criteria to decide which ones require treatment. What is this step called?
options: Risk avoidance
Risk evaluation
Risk identification
Risk transfer
items.explanation: Risk evaluation compares analyzed risks against criteria such as appetite to determine which need treatment. Identification surfaces the risks, while transfer and avoidance are response options chosen afterward.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a threat from a vulnerability?
options: A threat is a weakness in a system
A vulnerability is always an external attacker
A threat is a potential cause of harm, while a vulnerability is a weakness a threat can exploit
A threat and a vulnerability are exact synonyms
items.explanation: A threat is any potential source of harm and a vulnerability is an internal weakness that a threat may exploit. Conflating the two, calling a threat a weakness, or calling a vulnerability an attacker misunderstands the relationship.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Why should an organization select a risk assessment methodology before performing the assessment?
options: To delay the project until the budget is spent
To avoid having to document any results
To guarantee that no risks will be found
To ensure the identification, analysis, and evaluation are consistent and repeatable
items.explanation: A defined methodology makes assessments consistent across teams and comparable over time. Delay, lack of documentation, and finding no risk are not legitimate objectives of a methodology.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: When is a qualitative risk assessment most appropriate?
options: When rapid prioritization is needed and precise numeric values are unavailable
When an exact monetary loss figure must be produced
When no professional judgment may be applied
When regulators accept only quantitative results
items.explanation: Qualitative assessment uses descriptive scales and judgment, which is suitable for quick prioritization when hard numbers are lacking. A precise monetary figure, no judgment, or a quantitative-only mandate calls for quantitative methods.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: What is the main purpose of ranking risks during a risk assessment?
options: To remove the need for any controls
To focus treatment and limited resources on the most significant risks
To hide the low risks from management
To increase the total number of risks recorded
items.explanation: Ranking separates significant from minor risks so effort and money are directed where they matter most. Hiding risks, inflating counts, and dropping controls are not legitimate purposes.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Several individually small risks combine to create a significant exposure. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Risk avoidance
Risk acceptance
Risk aggregation
Risk transfer
items.explanation: Risk aggregation is the combining of many individual risks into a larger cumulative exposure. Transfer, avoidance, and acceptance are response choices, not the combining effect.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: A risk practitioner wants to determine whether an existing control reduces risk as intended. What should be assessed?
options: The vendor's share price
The visual design of the application
The layout of the office
The effectiveness of the control in reducing likelihood or impact
items.explanation: Control effectiveness is measured by whether the control actually reduces the likelihood or impact it was designed for. Financial, cosmetic, and facilities factors are unrelated to that determination.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: What is the purpose of assigning a risk owner during a risk assessment?
options: To make a specific person accountable for managing that risk
To automatically transfer the risk to another party
To remove the risk from the register
To increase the likelihood of the risk occurring
items.explanation: A risk owner is the individual accountable for monitoring and treating a risk. Ownership does not transfer the risk, delete it, or change its probability.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Why should risk assessments be repeated periodically rather than performed only once?
options: Because repetition is a purely cosmetic exercise
Because threats, vulnerabilities, business context, and controls change over time
Because regulators forbid performing a single assessment
Because risks never persist beyond the first assessment
items.explanation: The risk landscape is dynamic, so a one-time assessment becomes stale as the environment, threats, and controls evolve. Regular reassessment keeps the risk picture accurate and actionable.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: What is the foundation of an effective IT risk assessment?
options: The corporate phone directory
The annual marketing budget
A current inventory of information assets and an understanding of their value
A list of employee birthdays
items.explanation: You cannot assess the risk to assets you do not know exist or value, so an up-to-date asset inventory is foundational. The other items have no bearing on IT risk.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: How does a vulnerability assessment differ from a risk assessment?
options: A vulnerability assessment and a risk assessment are identical
A vulnerability assessment ignores all technical flaws
A risk assessment only produces a list of hosts
A vulnerability assessment identifies weaknesses, while a risk assessment determines business impact and prioritizes them
items.explanation: A vulnerability assessment enumerates technical weaknesses, while a risk assessment adds context such as business impact, likelihood, and priority. Treating them as identical misses the business dimension.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: During risk evaluation, how should the stated risk appetite be used?
options: As the benchmark for deciding whether a risk is acceptable or requires treatment
As a substitute for performing any impact analysis
As a document that is filed away and ignored
As a justification for disregarding the findings
items.explanation: Appetite is the yardstick against which evaluated risks are judged acceptable or in need of treatment. Using it as a substitute for analysis or as reason to ignore findings subverts its purpose.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Why is data classification important for risk assessment?
options: It selects the hardware brand to purchase
It helps determine the protection appropriate to the value and sensitivity of the data
It determines the salary levels of employees
It assigns office space to each department
items.explanation: Classification groups data by sensitivity and value so that protection and handling match the risk. It has no relation to salaries, office allocation, or hardware brand selection.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Which analysis identifies critical business processes and the impact of their disruption?
options: Penetration test
Network scan
Business impact analysis
Source code review
items.explanation: A business impact analysis identifies critical processes and quantifies the effect of their disruption, informing recovery priorities. Code review, penetration testing, and scanning address technical weaknesses, not business impact.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: What is the purpose of a risk heat map?
options: To replace the risk register entirely
To encrypt the organization's data
To assign user passwords automatically
To visually communicate likelihood and impact so risks can be prioritized
items.explanation: A heat map plots risks by likelihood and impact to give a quick visual prioritization for decision makers. It complements, rather than replaces, the register and performs no security function.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: A metric warns of increasing risk exposure before any losses occur. What type of indicator is this?
options: A leading indicator
A lagging indicator
A financial statement line
A physical control
items.explanation: A leading indicator moves ahead of the risk event and provides early warning. A lagging indicator reflects losses that have already happened, and neither a financial statement nor a control is an indicator.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: When assessing third-party risk, which factors should be evaluated?
options: The color scheme used on the vendor's website
The vendor's control environment, financial stability, and concentration risk
Only the vendor's glossy marketing materials
The number of social media followers the vendor has
items.explanation: Third-party risk depends on the vendor's control environment, financial health, and how concentrated the dependence is. Marketing, social following, and website design do not reflect the actual risk.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Why should emerging technologies receive a risk assessment before adoption?
options: To avoid having to document the decision
To deliberately raise the deployment cost
To understand new threats and control gaps that are not yet well understood
Because emerging technologies are always risk free
items.explanation: New technology brings unfamiliar threats and immature controls, so assessing it first lets the organization make an informed adoption decision. Assuming it is safe or skipping documentation leaves hidden exposure.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: What is the FIRST step in performing a risk assessment?
options: Purchase new security software immediately
Hire an external auditor to observe
Implement controls before any analysis
Define the scope, objectives, and criteria of the assessment
items.explanation: Scoping defines what is being assessed, why, and against what criteria, so later work is focused and comparable. Buying tools, hiring auditors, or implementing controls before scoping is premature.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: In risk assessment, what does a control gap analysis compare?
options: The controls that exist against the controls needed to reduce risk to acceptable levels
The prices charged by two competing vendors
The skill levels of employees only
The marketing strategies of the business units
items.explanation: A gap analysis identifies where current controls fall short of what is needed to bring risk within appetite. Vendor prices, employee skills, and marketing strategies are unrelated to control coverage.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Which technique systematically examines a system from an adversary's perspective to find design weaknesses?
options: Physical inventory counting
Threat modeling
Payroll processing
Manual data entry
items.explanation: Threat modeling maps potential attacks against a system's design to reveal weaknesses early. Payroll, data entry, and inventory counting are unrelated operational activities.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: Why is it important to consider dependencies and interdependencies among risks?
options: Because audits require a random sample of risks
Because it reduces the number of systems to assess
Because one risk event can trigger or amplify others across related systems
Because risks never interact with one another
items.explanation: Interdependencies mean a single event can cascade through connected systems, so correlated effects must be modeled. Ignoring these links understates the true exposure.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: What should be documented to support the conclusions of a risk assessment?
options: Only the final name of the highest risk
The auditor's personal lunch schedule
Nothing, in order to save time
The methodology, data sources, assumptions, and rationale for conclusions
items.explanation: Documenting methodology, sources, assumptions, and rationale makes the assessment repeatable and defensible. Recording only a name or nothing at all provides no basis for review or challenge.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: A risk evaluates as within tolerance on its own. What should still be considered before formally accepting it?
options: Its contribution to aggregated and correlated risk
The chief executive's personal opinion alone
The vendor's latest marketing claims
The total number of controls implemented
items.explanation: Even a small individual risk can push total exposure beyond appetite once aggregated or correlated with others. Personal opinion, marketing, and control counts do not substitute for that analysis.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - IT Risk Assessment

items.stem: After evaluating a risk, a practitioner must decide how the organization will address it. What is this decision called?
options: Risk capacity
Risk response
Risk identification
Risk appetite
items.explanation: Risk response is the selection and implementation of a treatment for an evaluated risk. Identification finds the risk, while appetite and capacity are governance limits, not responses.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: A company stops offering a service entirely because the associated risk cannot be reduced to an acceptable level. Which response is this?
options: Risk transfer
Risk acceptance
Risk avoidance
Risk mitigation
items.explanation: Avoidance eliminates the risk by exiting the activity that generates it. Mitigation reduces but keeps the activity, transfer shares it, and acceptance retains it.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: An organization adds monitoring controls and backups to lower the likelihood and impact of a risk. Which response is this?
options: Risk avoidance
Risk acceptance
Risk exploitation
Risk mitigation
items.explanation: Mitigation reduces risk through controls while continuing the activity. Avoidance exits it, acceptance retains it unchanged, and exploitation deliberately increases it for gain.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: A firm buys cyber insurance to cover potential breach losses. Which response is this?
options: Risk transfer
Risk avoidance
Risk mitigation
Risk acceptance
items.explanation: Insurance is a risk-transfer response that shifts the financial consequence to a third party. It does not avoid the event or reduce its likelihood as mitigation does.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: Management decides that a small residual risk is tolerable and continues the activity without further change. Which response is this?
options: Risk elimination
Risk acceptance
Risk avoidance
Risk transfer
items.explanation: Acceptance is a deliberate decision to retain a risk within appetite, with visibility and ownership. It is not avoidance, transfer, or elimination, since the risk remains present.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What is the most important factor when selecting a risk response?
options: Whether the response uses the newest technology available
Choosing the option with the shortest acronym
The organization's risk appetite and tolerance and the cost versus benefit of the response
The response preferred by the IT team without further analysis
items.explanation: Response selection weighs the treatment against appetite and the economics of benefit versus cost. Internal preference, novelty, and acronym length are not decision criteria.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: A proposed control costs more than the expected loss it would prevent. What should the risk practitioner advise?
options: Always implement it regardless of the cost
Ignore the cost entirely when deciding
Transfer the risk and forget the analysis
Reconsider the control because its cost may exceed the benefit it delivers
items.explanation: Proportionality matters, so a control whose cost exceeds the loss it prevents is generally not worthwhile unless required by law. Implementing blindly or ignoring cost wastes resources.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: A control stops an error or attack before it can occur. What type of control is this?
options: Preventive
Detective
Corrective
Compensating
items.explanation: Preventive controls stop an event before it happens, such as a firewall or input validation. Detective controls find it afterward, corrective controls fix it, and compensating controls substitute for a primary control.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: A control identifies an error after it has already occurred. What type of control is this?
options: Deterrent
Detective
Preventive
Corrective
items.explanation: Detective controls discover errors or incidents after the fact, such as logs or reconciliations. Preventive controls block them, corrective controls repair them, and deterrent controls discourage them.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: A control restores data after a failure or reverses a bad transaction. What type of control is this?
options: Detective
Directive
Corrective
Preventive
items.explanation: Corrective controls restore normal operations or reverse effects after an event. Preventive, detective, and directive controls act before or during events rather than repairing the aftermath.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: A visible warning banner that discourages misuse of a system is best described as which type of control?
options: Corrective
Detective
Preventive
Deterrent
items.explanation: Deterrent controls discourage a person from attempting an action by making consequences known. A banner does not technically block, detect, or repair the action.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: The primary control cannot be implemented yet, so management adds an alternative control in the interim. What is this called?
options: A compensating control
An unnecessary control
A transferred control
A residual control
items.explanation: A compensating control provides an alternative safeguard while the primary control is unavailable or impractical. It is not redundant, transferred, or the same as residual risk.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What is the difference between control design and control operating effectiveness?
options: Operating effectiveness concerns only the cost of the control
Design is whether a control can meet its objective, while operating effectiveness is whether it actually worked over time
Design and operating effectiveness mean exactly the same thing
Design refers to testing and effectiveness refers to planning
items.explanation: A control can be well designed yet fail in practice, so design and operating effectiveness are distinct test objectives. Treating them as identical or confusing them with cost misstates control assurance.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: How is the effectiveness of a key control typically verified?
options: By relying solely on the vendor's sales claims
By reading the vendor's marketing material
By testing the control and collecting supporting evidence
By assuming that it works because it was deployed
items.explanation: Control effectiveness is established through testing and evidence, not assumption or vendor assurance. Deployment alone does not prove the control operates as intended.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What is the main benefit of continuous monitoring over a single annual review?
options: It removes the need for any controls
It eliminates all residual risk immediately
It is purely a cosmetic improvement
It detects control failures and risk changes promptly rather than months later
items.explanation: Continuous monitoring shortens the time between a failure and its detection so remediation can start sooner. It does not remove controls, erase risk, or merely look better.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What is the role of a key risk indicator in a risk management program?
options: A metric that provides early warning of increasing risk exposure
A financial audit opinion issued by the auditor
A specific model of server hardware
A document used to procure goods
items.explanation: A key risk indicator is a measurable signal that tracks changes in risk exposure, ideally before losses occur. Audit opinions, hardware models, and purchase documents are not indicators.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What should accompany each key risk indicator so that it is actionable?
options: An unrelated decorative chart
A defined threshold or trigger that prompts a response
A completely random numeric value
A marketing slogan attached to it
items.explanation: A KRI becomes actionable when a threshold defines when and how the organization reacts. Random values, slogans, and decorative charts provide no decision trigger.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: How does a key risk indicator differ from a key performance indicator?
options: A key performance indicator is used only by external auditors
A key risk indicator is always a financial measure
A key risk indicator signals risk exposure while a key performance indicator measures progress against objectives
A key risk indicator and a key performance indicator are the same thing
items.explanation: KRIs warn about risk exposure, whereas KPIs measure performance toward objectives, and some metrics can serve both roles. Treating them as identical or as auditor or finance only tools is incorrect.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What is the PRIMARY objective of risk reporting to stakeholders?
options: To hide unfavorable news from decision makers
To maximize the length of the report
To assign blame for past failures
To provide timely, accurate information that supports informed risk decisions
items.explanation: Risk reporting exists to give stakeholders the information they need to make sound decisions. Concealing bad news, padding length, and assigning blame undermine that objective.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: When reporting risk to the board, what level of detail is most appropriate?
options: A concise summary of material risks, trends, and the decisions needed
Every low-level technical log entry produced by the systems
Only raw vulnerability counts with no context
No context and no recommendations whatsoever
items.explanation: Boards need material risks, trends, and choices presented concisely so they can govern. Raw technical detail or unexplained numbers bury the decisions that require board attention.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What is the purpose of a risk dashboard?
options: To process supplier invoices
To present key risk metrics and trends at a glance for decision makers
To securely store user passwords
To replace the risk register permanently
items.explanation: A dashboard condenses key metrics and trends so leaders can quickly assess status and act. It does not store credentials, replace the register, or process payments.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: After a risk response is implemented, what should be updated to reflect the new position?
options: The company org chart only
Nothing at all should be updated
The risk register, including residual risk and control status
The annual marketing plan
items.explanation: The register should capture the new residual risk and control status so reporting stays accurate. Marketing plans, org charts, and inaction leave the record misleading.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What should a risk treatment plan specify?
options: Only the name of the risk being addressed
The vendor's street address
The physical location of the data center
The actions, owners, timelines, and expected residual risk
items.explanation: A treatment plan defines what will be done, by whom, by when, and the expected residual risk, making it trackable. A bare name or unrelated address provides no plan.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: Who should formally accept a residual risk that exceeds the defined appetite?
options: The appropriate senior authority or governance body under the authority matrix
A junior analyst working on the project
An external vendor supplying a component
The help desk technician on duty
items.explanation: Accepting risk above appetite requires authority commensurate with the exposure, normally a senior executive or governance body. Delegating it downward undermines accountability and governance.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: Why must each risk response have a clearly assigned owner?
options: To avoid having to report on the risk
To ensure accountability for executing and monitoring the response
To transfer legal liability to that person automatically
To remove the risk from the register
items.explanation: An assigned owner is accountable for carrying out and monitoring the response so it does not stall. Ownership does not shift legal liability, delete the risk, or excuse reporting.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: When should a risk response be implemented relative to the urgency of the risk?
options: Whenever it is convenient for the team
It should never be implemented at all
In line with the risk's priority and any applicable regulatory deadlines
Only after the following annual audit cycle
items.explanation: Response timing should match the risk's severity and any legal deadlines so urgent exposures are addressed promptly. Waiting for convenience or the next audit leaves significant risk unmanaged.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What is the benefit of planning control implementation in phases?
options: It delays all benefit indefinitely with no reason
It removes accountability for the controls
It guarantees that no incidents will occur
It manages complexity and cost while addressing the highest risks first
items.explanation: Phasing lets the organization tackle the most significant risks early while spreading cost and effort. It does not eliminate accountability or guarantee incident-free operation.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: How often should control effectiveness be reassessed after implementation?
options: At a frequency based on the risk and control criticality, with continuous monitoring where feasible
Once at implementation and then never again
Once every ten years regardless of the risk
Only after a major incident has already happened
items.explanation: Reassessment frequency should reflect the criticality of the control and the risk it addresses, supported by monitoring. Testing once, rarely, or only after a failure allows undetected degradation.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: When must a risk event be reported to a regulator?
options: Whenever a competitor publicly reports an event
When laws or regulations require notification of specified events such as breaches or control failures
Never, because regulators have no interest in events
Only when the company's share price rises significantly
items.explanation: Mandatory reporting is triggered by legal or regulatory requirements, often with strict timelines. There is no general rule to report never, on share-price moves, or to mirror a competitor.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: A control exception is discovered that raises risk above tolerance. What should happen next?
options: Delete the supporting evidence
Wait until a customer complains before acting
Escalate promptly through the defined governance process
Ignore it until the next annual review
items.explanation: Exceptions that push risk beyond tolerance require prompt escalation so the risk can be treated or formally accepted. Ignoring, destroying evidence, or waiting for a complaint lets exposure grow.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: A key risk indicator has breached its defined threshold. What is the expected governance action?
options: Take no action and continue as before
Quietly raise the threshold to avoid escalation
Hide the metric from the report
Trigger the pre-defined escalation and response so the risk is addressed
items.explanation: A threshold breach should activate the planned escalation and response. Ignoring it, moving the goalposts, or concealing the metric defeats the purpose of a KRI.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What is the purpose of incident reporting within risk management?
options: To capture events, root causes, and lessons that inform future risk assessment and response
To assign all blame to the IT department
To avoid having to file insurance claims
To reduce the amount of documentation required
items.explanation: Incident reports feed lessons learned back into assessment and response so the same failure is less likely to recur. Blame, claims avoidance, and less documentation are not their purpose.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: Why is loss event data valuable for risk management?
options: It is useful only to the accounting department
It provides empirical evidence that helps calibrate likelihood and impact estimates
It removes the need for any controls going forward
It guarantees what future results will be
items.explanation: Historical loss data grounds estimates in observed experience, improving the accuracy of likelihood and impact. It does not replace controls or guarantee future outcomes.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What determines the appropriate frequency of risk reporting?
options: The color of the paper used for the report
A fixed rule of once every ten years
The risk's velocity and materiality and the information needs of decision makers
The personal schedule of whoever writes the report
items.explanation: Reporting cadence should match how fast risks can materialize and how much they matter to those governing. Personal convenience, formatting, and arbitrary intervals do not serve decision needs.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What makes a risk metric meaningful to management?
options: It is deliberately complex and left unexplained
Its definition changes unpredictably each month
It is always reported as a value of zero
It is tied to objectives, actionable, and clearly defined
items.explanation: A meaningful metric connects to objectives, can drive action, and is defined consistently. Complexity without explanation, shifting definitions, and permanently zero values provide no decision value.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: Why is aggregation important when reporting enterprise risk?
options: It reveals the combined exposure across business units that separate reports can hide
It reduces accountability for individual risks
It replaces the need for mitigation entirely
It conceals all risks from the board
items.explanation: Aggregating risk shows the cumulative enterprise exposure that unit-level views may obscure. It does not erase accountability, remove mitigation, or hide risks.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: How should a risk practitioner communicate a technical risk to business stakeholders?
options: By sending only raw packet captures
In business terms, describing the potential impact on objectives and operations
Using unexplained technical jargon with no translation
By refusing to explain the risk at all
items.explanation: Business stakeholders act on consequences to objectives, so translating technical exposure into impact is essential. Jargon, refusal, or raw data prevents informed decisions.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What is the purpose of a control self-assessment?
options: To replace risk ownership across the enterprise
To eliminate the need for any documentation
To let business and process owners evaluate and attest to their own controls
To outsource all control testing to an external party
items.explanation: Control self-assessment engages process owners in evaluating their controls, strengthening ownership and coverage. It complements rather than replaces independent testing or ownership.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: After mitigation, how should the residual risk be reported to management?
options: As though the risk had been completely eliminated
Without any context or comparison to appetite
Only to the external vendor involved
Along with the mitigation applied and any remaining exposure against appetite
items.explanation: Management needs to see what was done and what exposure remains relative to appetite. Reporting the risk as eliminated, without context, or only to a vendor is misleading.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: How should risk responses differ for critical third parties compared with low-risk suppliers?
options: Critical third parties should be held to contractual control requirements and monitored through ongoing reporting and audits
Critical third parties should be exempt from all control requirements
Critical third parties should self-report with no verification
Critical third parties should be removed from all oversight
items.explanation: The greater the dependence, the stronger the contractual controls and ongoing monitoring required. Exempting critical vendors, accepting unverified self-reporting, or dropping oversight increases exposure.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: How does business continuity planning function as a risk response?
options: It guarantees that downtime never occurs
It reduces the impact of disruptive events by enabling timely recovery
It eliminates all threats to the organization
It transfers risk entirely to insurers
items.explanation: Continuity planning lowers the impact of disruption by restoring critical functions within agreed timeframes. It does not remove threats, transfer risk, or guarantee zero downtime.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: In which situation is risk transfer through insurance LEAST effective?
options: When a valid policy has been signed
When the losses are purely financial in nature
When the loss involves reputation, customer trust, or regulatory penalties that cannot be insured
When the premium has been paid in full
items.explanation: Insurance compensates financial loss but cannot restore reputation, trust, or shield against regulatory penalties. Purely financial losses are the losses insurance handles best.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: Why must a decision to accept risk be documented?
options: To deliberately increase the level of the risk
To avoid any need for future governance
To satisfy the personal curiosity of staff
To provide evidence of informed, authorized acceptance and accountability
items.explanation: Documentation proves the acceptance was informed and authorized by the right level of management. It does not change the risk level, remove governance, or serve curiosity.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What should management do when reviewing a risk report?
options: Make and record decisions on treatment, acceptance, and resource allocation
File it away without reading it
Forward it to a competitor for comparison
Delete it as soon as it arrives
items.explanation: The purpose of a risk report is to provoke and record decisions. Filing without reading, sharing with competitors, or deleting it renders the reporting cycle pointless.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: How should low-probability, high-impact risks be handled in risk reporting?
options: They should be excluded from the risk framework
They should be explicitly considered so governance remains aware of tail risk
They should be ignored because they are unlikely to occur
They should always be accepted silently with no record
items.explanation: Tail risks can be catastrophic if they occur, so governance should be aware of them even when likelihood is low. Ignoring, silently accepting, or excluding them leaves the board blind to severe scenarios.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: What is the purpose of tracking corrective actions after an audit or incident?
options: To assign punitive penalties to staff
To close findings without any supporting evidence
To ensure agreed remediation is completed and actually reduces the risk
To generate paperwork with no practical value
items.explanation: Tracking corrective actions verifies remediation is completed and effective so the risk is genuinely reduced. Paperwork, punishment, and evidence-free closure defeat the purpose.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: A critical control repeatedly fails while the business still depends on it. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?
options: Ignore the failures because the control exists
Disable the control to prevent further failures
Accept the risk without any review or authority
Implement a compensating control while the root cause is corrected
items.explanation: A compensating control limits exposure while the failing control's root cause is fixed. Ignoring, disabling, or unauthorized acceptance would increase risk during a known control weakness.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: How does risk information support risk-adjusted decision making?
options: It lets leaders weigh expected return against residual risk and appetite
It fully replaces financial analysis in every case
It removes all uncertainty from decisions
It forbids making any trade-offs
items.explanation: Risk information lets decision makers balance potential return against residual risk and appetite. It complements rather than replaces financial analysis and cannot eliminate uncertainty.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Risk Response and Reporting

items.stem: When reviewing a proposed system architecture, which risk concern is MOST important?
options: The interior decoration of the data center
Whether the design meets security, resilience, and business requirements
Whether the technology is currently popular
The size of the vendor's marketing budget
items.explanation: Architecture risk review focuses on whether the design satisfies security, resilience, and business needs. Popularity, marketing spend, and decor do not address architectural risk.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: Which access principle grants users only the permissions needed to perform their assigned duties?
options: Mandatory vacation
Job rotation
Least privilege
Separation of duties
items.explanation: Least privilege limits access to the minimum required for the role, reducing misuse and blast radius. Separation of duties, vacation, and rotation are complementary fraud controls, not the least-access principle.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: What is the main goal of identity and access management?
options: To process employee payroll accurately
To design and build network cabling
To write policy documents only
To ensure the right people have the right access to the right resources and that it can be audited
items.explanation: IAM manages identities and entitlements so access is appropriate and reviewable. Payroll, cabling, and documentation are separate functions, though policy may guide IAM.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: Why is privileged access management especially important for risk?
options: Administrative accounts can bypass controls and cause the greatest damage if compromised
Administrative accounts are rarely used and carry little risk
Administrative accounts cannot access sensitive systems
Administrative credentials are normally public information
items.explanation: Privileged accounts hold the keys to the environment, so their compromise or misuse has outsized impact. Assuming they are low-risk, powerless, or public is dangerously wrong.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: Combining something a user knows with something the user possesses is an example of what?
options: Data masking
Multi-factor authentication
Single sign-on
Least privilege
items.explanation: Multi-factor authentication combines different factor types, such as a password plus a hardware token. Single sign-on, least privilege, and data masking address different concerns.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: Why is network segmentation valuable for managing risk?
options: It removes any need for firewalls
It automatically encrypts all stored data
It limits lateral movement and helps contain the impact of a compromise
It increases the size of broadcast domains deliberately
items.explanation: Segmentation divides the network so an intruder cannot easily move sideways, containing damage. It does not enlarge broadcast domains, replace firewalls, or encrypt data at rest.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: What is the primary function of a firewall in risk terms?
options: To store nightly backup copies of databases
To assign IP addresses to endpoints
To print administrative reports
To enforce network access rules and reduce exposure between zones
items.explanation: A firewall controls traffic flows between zones according to policy, reducing exposure. Backups, address assignment, and printing are functions of other systems.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: How do encryption at rest and encryption in transit differ?
options: At rest protects stored data, while in transit protects data moving across networks
They are exactly the same control applied twice
In transit protects files sitting on disk
At rest protects signals traveling on cables
items.explanation: Encryption at rest protects data while stored, and encryption in transit protects it as it crosses networks. Reversing them or treating them as identical misstates where the protection applies.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: Why is cryptographic key management a critical control?
options: Because it removes the need for access control
Because poorly managed keys allow encrypted data to be exposed
Because encryption keys are meant to be public
Because keys never need to be rotated
items.explanation: The strength of encryption depends on keys remaining secret, available, and rotated, so weak key management breaks the protection. Keys are not public, do need rotation, and do not replace access control.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: When should security requirements first be introduced in the system development life cycle?
options: Only during the annual audit cycle
Only after a security incident occurs
From the earliest requirements and design phases
Only after the system has gone live
items.explanation: Building security in from requirements and design is cheaper and more effective than retrofitting later. Adding it after go-live, at audit, or after an incident is costly and incomplete.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: What is the purpose of secure coding practices?
options: To make the code longer and harder to read
To remove the need for any testing
To deliberately reduce system functionality
To reduce vulnerabilities such as injection flaws and insecure defaults in software
items.explanation: Secure coding prevents common vulnerability classes at the source. It does not exist to inflate code, remove testing, or reduce functionality.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: An organization processes the personal data of European Union residents. Which regulation governs this processing?
options: The General Data Protection Regulation
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act
The Basel III Accord
The ISO 9001 standard
items.explanation: The GDPR governs the processing of personal data of EU residents. Sarbanes-Oxley concerns financial reporting, Basel III concerns banking capital, and ISO 9001 is a quality management standard.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: Why is a data retention policy important for managing risk?
options: It ensures data is never deleted under any circumstance
It limits legal, privacy, and storage risk by defining how long data is kept
It increases the volume of data the organization stores
It removes all privacy obligations from the organization
items.explanation: Retention rules reduce the legal and privacy exposure of holding data too long while preserving what must be kept. They do not remove obligations or mandate keeping everything forever.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: What is the purpose of data loss prevention controls?
options: To create regular backups of databases
To assign user passwords automatically
To detect and block unauthorized transmission of sensitive data
To speed up the internal network
items.explanation: Data loss prevention monitors and stops sensitive data from leaving authorized boundaries. Network speed, backups, and password assignment are unrelated functions.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: What does a recovery time objective define?
options: The acceptable amount of data loss measured in time
The amount of the insurance payout after an outage
The deadline for completing the annual audit
The target time within which a process must be restored after disruption
items.explanation: The recovery time objective is the target elapsed time to restore a process after disruption. The acceptable data loss is the recovery point objective, and insurance and audit deadlines are unrelated.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: What does a recovery point objective define?
options: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time
The time required to restore service after an outage
The duration of a scheduled maintenance window
The cost incurred for each hour of downtime
items.explanation: The recovery point objective expresses how much data the organization can afford to lose, measured in time, and drives backup frequency. Restore time is the RTO, and cost or maintenance windows are separate measures.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: Why should disaster recovery plans be tested regularly?
options: To reduce the number of backups that are taken
To verify that recovery is achievable within the defined RTO and RPO
To satisfy the personal curiosity of the team
To deliberately delay the recovery process
items.explanation: Testing proves that recovery can actually meet the stated time and data-loss objectives and reveals gaps. Curiosity, delay, and fewer backups are not the reasons to test.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: How does business continuity differ from disaster recovery?
options: Disaster recovery covers only the safety of people
Business continuity covers only the recovery of hardware
Business continuity keeps critical business functions running, while disaster recovery restores IT systems and data
Business continuity and disaster recovery mean exactly the same thing
items.explanation: Business continuity focuses on sustaining critical business functions during disruption, whereas disaster recovery focuses on restoring IT infrastructure and data. They are related but distinct disciplines.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: Under the cloud shared responsibility model, what generally remains the customer's responsibility?
options: The physical security of the provider's data centers
The security of the provider's underlying hypervisor
Nothing at all, because the provider covers everything
Security of their data, identities, and configuration in the cloud
items.explanation: The customer remains responsible for its data, identities, access, and configuration, while the provider secures the underlying infrastructure. Assuming the provider covers everything is a common and dangerous error.
items.reference: ISACA CRISC Exam Content Outline - Technology and Security

items.stem: Which risk is introduced by rapid cloud adoption without appropriate governance?
options: Unmanaged data residency, misconfiguration, and loss of visibility
Guaranteed regulatory compliance in every jurisdiction
A reduced overall attack surface
The complete elimination of insider risk
